q.q: A banking system has a 10 percent reserve requirement, but banks hold an additional 5 percent of deposits as excess reserves and the public holds no currency. A simple effective deposit multiplier is closest to:
q.commonError: Ignoring voluntary excess reserves.
q.feedback: If 15 percent of deposits is retained, the simple effective multiplier is about 1/0.15 = 6.67.

q.q: If excess reserves are $25,000, actual reserves are $85,000, and the reserve ratio is 12 percent, what are deposits?
q.commonError: forgetting to find required reserves before solving deposits
q.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $85,000 - $25,000 = $60,000. Deposits = $60,000 / 0.12 = $500,000.

q.q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a required reserve ratio of 12.5 percent, and actual reserves of $140,000. How much can it lend before hitting its required reserve level?
q.commonError: treating all actual reserves as lendable reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $800,000 = $100,000. Excess reserves are $140,000 - $100,000 = $40,000.

q.q: A simplified fiscal account reports gross tax receipts of $900 billion, transfers of $180 billion, government purchases of $660 billion and interest payments of $70 billion. These are all revenues and outlays. For this exercise define T as gross taxes minus transfers, excluding interest. Which pair gives textbook public saving T − G and the full budget balance?
options: Public saving is $240 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
Public saving is −$10 billion; the full budget also has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $10 billion deficit
Public saving is $60 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Public saving is $240 billion; the full budget has a $60 billion surplus” in this budget accounting and public saving task.
q.feedback: Under the stated convention, T = 900 − 180 = $720 billion and T − G = $60 billion. Total outlays are 180 + 660 + 70 = $910 billion, giving a $10 billion deficit. The $70 billion difference is interest, which this exercise excludes from net taxes. Transfers are already deducted in T and must not be deducted a second time.

q.q: T is net tax revenue of $700 billion and G is purchases of $600 billion. What is public saving?
options: −$100 billion
+$100 billion
$600 billion
$1.3 trillion
q.commonError: Reverses revenues minus spending, giving public saving or the budget balance the wrong sign.
q.feedback: Subtract government purchases from net tax revenue: $700 billion minus $600 billion equals +$100 billion.

q.q: Why does negative public saving matter beyond the federal budget?
options: It directly fixes the economy's nominal exchange rate
It makes positive private saving impossible by definition
It reduces one component of national saving
It determines the national money supply without monetary policy
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It directly fixes the economy's nominal exchange rate” in this budget accounting and public saving task.
q.feedback: Negative public saving lowers national saving, all else equal, and therefore reduces the funds available to finance investment in the loanable-funds model.

q.q: Domestic real returns rise while perceived domestic political risk also rises. An analyst observes that NCO increased and concludes that higher interest rates caused capital flight. Holding other determinants fixed, which inference separates the observed change from the interest-rate effect?
options: The positive NCO response proves that higher domestic rates increase desired foreign purchases
The identity NX = NCO requires risk and interest-rate effects to have equal size
The risk-driven outward shift dominated the rate-induced reduction in NCO; the observation does not reverse the rate mechanism
The rate increase must have preceded the risk shock because NCO rose
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The positive NCO response proves that higher domestic rates increase desired foreign purchases” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
q.feedback: The return effect lowers NCO, while the domestic risk shock raises it. Positive net change under these two channels shows that risk dominated, not that the partial interest-rate slope reversed. Timing is not identified.

q.q: Planned private saving rises by $30 billion and public saving falls by $10 billion at each real rate. What happens to investment in the loanable-funds model if investment demand is unchanged?
options: Lower national saving raises the real rate and reduces investment along the existing demand curve.
Higher national saving lowers the real rate and raises investment along the existing demand curve.
The $20 billion net saving increase shifts investment demand right and raises the real rate.
Investment is unchanged because opposing saving changes must cancel completely.
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving falls $40 billion, shifting supply left and reducing investment” in this crowding out and capital formation task.
q.feedback: The net national-saving increase is $20 billion at a given rate. Supply shifts right, lowering the real rate and encouraging investment along its unchanged demand curve.

q.q: A budget improvement raises planned public saving by $25 billion while private saving falls by $10 billion at each real rate. An analyst says this directly raises firms' investment demand. How should that claim be corrected?
options: National saving rises $15 billion; investment demand shifts right because all additional saving is a new project.
National saving falls $35 billion; supply shifts left and investment falls.
National saving is unchanged; any change in public saving is canceled by private saving.
National saving rises $15 billion; supply shifts right, and the lower rate induces investment along unchanged demand.
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving falls $35 billion, shifting supply left; the higher rate reduces investment” in this crowding out and capital formation task.
q.feedback: National saving rises by $15 billion at each rate, shifting supply right. The lower equilibrium real rate then increases investment along unchanged demand. A saving increase does not itself raise project profitability at every rate.

q.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the curves are straight. A budget improvement shifts S0 to S1; the private-saving schedule and investment demand are unchanged. What does the graph imply about the rise in public saving and the induced change in private saving between A and B?
options: Public saving rises $60 billion; lower rates induce a $20 billion decline in private saving.
Public saving rises $80 billion; lower rates induce a $40 billion decline in private saving.
Public saving rises $80 billion; the fixed private-saving schedule means private saving cannot change.
Public saving rises $40 billion; the equilibrium investment increase directly measures the policy-induced supply shift.
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Public saving rises $40 billion; private saving is unchanged because its schedule is fixed” in this crowding out and capital formation task.
q.feedback: The horizontal supply shift is 80 units: at an 8 percent rate S0 is at 60 and S1 is at 140. With the private-saving schedule unchanged, that shift is the $80 billion public-saving increase. Final national saving and investment rise only from 60 to 100, or $40 billion. Private saving consequently changes by 40 − 80 = −$40 billion through movement along its schedule as the rate falls.

q.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is labeled Quantity of loanable funds; the vertical axis is labeled Real interest rate. Coordinates below are (quantity, rate). The quantity axis has no currency scale. All curves are straight. The solid red line labeled S0 slopes upward through (0, 5) and (60, 8). The dashed red line labeled S1 slopes upward through (0, 1) and (100, 6). The solid blue line labeled D0 slopes downward through (0, 11) and (220, 0). Point A marks the S0–D0 intersection at (60, 8). Point B marks the S1–D0 intersection at (100, 6). A numbered grid provides the coordinate scale.

q.q: Two packages require the same additional borrowing, leave public saving equally lower, and face the same unchanged private-saving and investment-demand schedules. Package A finances productive public infrastructure; Package B finances transfers. What evidence is needed to decide whether A leaves more total productive capital than before the policy?
options: Whether the public-capital addition exceeds the private-capital formation displaced by the higher real rate
Whether A issues less debt than B, even though their additional borrowing is stated to be equal
Whether transfers count as current public-capital formation at the moment they are paid
Whether a decline in public saving is itself a one-for-one measure of lost private capital
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Whether A issues less debt than B, even though their additional borrowing is stated to be equal” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
q.feedback: Both packages create the same initial loanable-funds pressure under the stated schedules. A also adds public productive capital. Its net capital effect depends on that addition relative to displaced private capital formation; borrowing alone does not establish the sign. No project-valuation or AD-AS model is needed for this comparison.

q.q: Public debt starts at $200 and ends two years later at $260. The first-year budget deficit is $20. Assume deficits are financed entirely by borrowing and there are no other debt adjustments. An analyst calls the $260 ending debt the second-year deficit. What second-year deficit and correction follow?
options: $60; the entire two-year increase is the second-year deficit
$40; subtract initial debt and the first deficit from the ending stock
$260; an ending debt stock is the deficit for its final year
$240; subtract only the first-year deficit from ending debt
q.commonError: Treats the ending debt stock, or the whole two-year change, as a single-year deficit.
q.feedback: The two-year debt increase is 260−200=60. Subtract the known first-year deficit 20 to infer the missing second-year deficit 40. The ending stock includes earlier borrowing; it is not a one-year flow.

q.q: A deficit reduces public saving at every real rate. A separate household incentive exactly offsets that reduction in planned private saving at every rate, while an investment tax credit also raises desired investment. In the closed-economy loanable-funds model, what can be concluded relative to the initial equilibrium?
options: The saving curve shifts left; the real rate rises and private investment must fall
Both curves are unchanged; exact private-saving offset also cancels the investment tax credit
The saving curve is unchanged; the real rate and equilibrium private investment rise
The saving curve shifts right; private investment rises but the real rate must fall
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The saving curve shifts left; the real rate rises and private investment must fall” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
q.feedback: The public- and private-saving shifts cancel at every rate, leaving national-saving supply unchanged. The tax credit separately shifts investment demand right. With an upward-sloping saving curve, the new equilibrium has a higher real rate and more private investment. A higher rate alone does not prove crowding out when investment demand also changes.

q.q: A larger deficit reduces public saving while private saving is unchanged. In a closed-economy loanable-funds model with unchanged investment demand, what pressure does this place on interest and private investment?
options: Interest rises and private investment rises
Interest falls and private investment falls
Interest rises and private investment falls
Interest falls and private investment rises
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Interest rises and private investment rises” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
q.feedback: Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left. The higher equilibrium interest rate reduces investment demanded.

q.q: If the simple money multiplier falls from 10 to 4, what happened to the reserve ratio?
options: It rose from 10 percent to 25 percent.
It fell from 25 percent to 10 percent.
It rose from 4 percent to 10 percent.
It fell from 10 percent to 4 percent.
q.commonError: thinking a smaller multiplier means a smaller reserve ratio
q.feedback: The reserve ratio is 1/multiplier. A multiplier of 10 means 10 percent; a multiplier of 4 means 25 percent.

q.q: In a hypothetical system with a fixed 12.5 percent reserve ratio, a household deposits $28,000 of existing public currency. Banks initially have no excess reserves. Every bank lends all new excess reserves, all loan payments are redeposited, and no other constraint binds. An analyst counts the first deposit as new money and reports the full deposit increase as money creation. Which set of results diagnoses the error?
options: First loan $24,500; deposit increase $224,000; net money increase $196,000.
First loan $24,500; deposit increase $196,000; net money increase $224,000.
First loan $3,500; deposit increase $224,000; net money increase $224,000.
First loan $28,000; deposit increase $196,000; net money increase $168,000.
q.commonError: confusing first-round lending with total deposit expansion
q.feedback: The first loan is $28,000 × 0.875 = $24,500. Deposits rise by $28,000/0.125 = $224,000. Subtract the $28,000 decline in public currency to obtain $196,000 of net money creation.

q.q: In two hypothetical steady states, the public holds no currency and banks have a fixed required-reserve ratio of 10 percent. The observed deposit-to-reserve ratio falls from 8 to 5. Assume all reserves are either required or deliberately held as excess reserves. Which diagnosis fits both observations?
options: The excess-reserve share of deposits rose from 2.5 to 10 percent.
The required-reserve ratio rose from 12.5 to 20 percent.
The excess-reserve share of deposits fell from 10 to 2.5 percent.
The public currency-to-deposit ratio rose from 2.5 to 10 percent.
q.commonError: thinking a lower multiplier means a lower reserve ratio
q.feedback: Total reserves/deposits are the reciprocal of deposits/reserves: 12.5 percent, then 20 percent. Subtract the unchanged 10 percent requirement to infer excess-reserve shares of 2.5 and 10 percent.

q.q: In a hypothetical system, a household deposits $10,000 of currency previously held outside banks. Banks initially meet a fixed 20 percent reserve ratio exactly, lend every new excess reserve dollar, and all loan payments are redeposited without currency drain. No other constraint binds. What are the first bank’s loan and the eventual net increase in currency plus checking deposits?
options: First loan $8,000; net money increase $40,000.
First loan $8,000; net money increase $50,000.
First loan $2,000; net money increase $40,000.
First loan $10,000; net money increase $50,000.
q.commonError: confusing initial lending with total possible deposit creation
q.feedback: Required reserves on the initial deposit are $2,000, leaving an $8,000 first loan. Total deposits rise by $10,000/0.20 = $50,000, but public currency falls by $10,000. Net money creation is $40,000.

q.q: Use a hypothetical banking system initially holding exactly its required reserves. The stated reserve ratio stays fixed, banks lend all excess reserves, every loan payment is fully redeposited, and there is no currency drain or other lending constraint. The initial deposit comes from currency previously held by the public, and total deposit expansion includes that initial deposit. Suppose the reserve ratio is 25 percent and a public cash deposit of $4,000 enters the banking system. What is the maximum total deposit expansion and the first bank's initial loan?
options: Maximum expansion = $16,000; initial loan = $3,000
Maximum expansion = $4,000; initial loan = $1,000
Maximum expansion = $3,000; initial loan = $16,000
Maximum expansion = $1,000; initial loan = $4,000
q.commonError: confusing first-round loan with total deposit expansion
q.feedback: Multiplier is 1 / 0.25 = 4, so total expansion is $16,000. First bank keeps $1,000 and lends $3,000. The initial cash deposit itself replaces public currency with deposits; it is not net new money.

q.q: Banks receive $140 in new reserves. The required reserve ratio is 10%, which would give a simple deposit multiplier of 10 if banks held no excess reserves. Banks also choose to hold excess reserves equal to 10% of deposits. With no currency leakage, what is the maximum deposit increase supported by the new reserves?
options: $2800 in total deposits; add the reciprocals of the two ratios
$280 in total deposits; multiply reserves by the percentage expressed as 2
$700 in total deposits; the effective reserve fraction is 20%
$1400 in total deposits; excess reserves never constrain lending
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “$2800 in total deposits; add the reciprocals of the two ratios” in this deposit creation and money multiplier task.
q.feedback: Required plus additional reserves total 20% of deposits. Thus deposits supported by 140 new reserves are 140/.20 = 700, rather than the required-ratio-only maximum.

q.q: If the reserve requirement is 20 percent, the simple money multiplier is:
q.feedback: The simple multiplier is 1/reserve requirement, so 1/0.20 = 5.

q.commonError: Using the reserve ratio as the multiplier.
q.q: The simple money multiplier equals:
options: 1 divided by the reserve ratio
The reserve ratio divided by 1
Deposits minus reserves
M2 minus M1
q.feedback: The simple money multiplier is 1/r.

q.commonError: Using 0.20 as the multiplier when the reserve ratio is 20%.
q.q: If the reserve ratio is 20%, the simple multiplier is:

At a fixed price level, initial desired output is $500 billion. Government purchases rise by $40 billion and MPC is 0.5. Crowding out creates a total $20 billion AD offset, already including induced effects. Under the simple spending multiplier, what is the new quantity of output demanded?
options: $560 billion; subtract the already-total offset from the multiplied spending increase.
$540 billion; subtract the offset from purchases before multiplying both amounts.
$580 billion; the offset does not affect demand after the multiplier operates.
$620 billion; add the offset to the multiplied spending increase.
q.commonError: Confusing the initial shift with the multiplied shift.
q.feedback: The spending multiplier is 2, so the gross demand increase is $80 billion. Subtract the already-total $20 billion offset once, leaving a $60 billion net increase and $560 billion demanded. Without supply information, this is not a prediction of equilibrium output.

q.q: Fiscal expansion raises AD through the multiplier, but interest rates rise and investment falls. Which description best fits the final result?
options: Initial AD shift partly offset by crowding out
SRAS shift fully offset by lower taxes
LRPC shift partly offset by higher inflation
Money demand shift fully offset by M1
q.commonError: Treating the multiplier as the final effect every time.
q.feedback: Fiscal expansion can be amplified by the multiplier but weakened by crowding out.

q.q: If the initial AD shift is $30 billion and the final shift is $150 billion, what MPC is implied by the simple multiplier?
q.commonError: using final shift divided by initial shift as MPC instead of multiplier
q.feedback: The multiplier is 150/30 = 5. If 1/(1-MPC)=5, then MPC = 0.8.

q.q: If policymakers expect the multiplier shift to close a recessionary gap exactly, but crowding out is stronger than expected, what is the likely result?
options: AD does not shift far enough right to fully close the gap.
AD shifts too far right because crowding out magnifies fiscal policy.
AD shifts left because government spending is not part of AD.
The multiplier becomes infinite.
q.commonError: thinking crowding out strengthens the fiscal multiplier
q.feedback: Stronger crowding out reduces the net AD shift, so stimulus may fall short.

q.q: Government purchases increase by $60 billion. MPC = 0.75; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $50 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. What is the net rightward AD shift?
options: $190 billion
$240 billion
$110 billion
$10 billion
q.commonError: forgetting to apply the multiplier before subtracting crowding out
q.feedback: Multiplier is 4, so the gross shift is $240 billion. Subtract $50 billion crowding out for a net $190 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

q.q: Government purchases increase by $100 billion. MPC = 0.6; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $75 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. Which sequence separates the direct purchases, gross multiplier prediction, and net AD shift?
options: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $175 billion shift.
AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out increases it to $325 billion.
AD first shifts left $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $250 billion, then crowding out leaves $175 billion.
AD shifts right $100 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
q.commonError: adding crowding out instead of subtracting it from the gross multiplier shift
q.feedback: MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. The $100 billion initial shift becomes $250 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $175 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

q.q: Two governments each increase purchases by $60 billion. Economy A has MPC 0.80 and a total $100 billion reduction in aggregate demand from crowding out; Economy B has MPC 0.60 and a total $20 billion reduction. These offsets already include induced spending effects. Using the simple spending multiplier, which comparison is correct?
options: Economy A has a $200 billion net AD increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy B.
Economy A has a $300 billion net increase and Economy B has a $150 billion net increase because crowding out does not affect AD.
Economy B has a $200 billion net increase, which is $70 billion larger than Economy A.
Both economies have the same $180 billion net AD increase because the initial spending changes are equal.
q.commonError: Compares gross multiplier effects without subtracting the private spending displaced by higher interest rates.
q.feedback: A: 60/(1−0.80)−100 = 300−100 = $200 billion. B: 60/(1−0.60)−20 = 150−20 = $130 billion. A's net increase is $70 billion larger. Each stated crowding-out amount is already a total AD offset and is subtracted once, not multiplied again.

q.q: Government purchases rise by $80 billion and MPC is 0.75. The observed net AD increase is $230 billion. Define crowding out here as the total reduction in AD after induced spending effects, not an autonomous investment change. How much of the gross spending-multiplier effect was offset?
options: $230 billion.
$320 billion.
$10 billion.
$90 billion.
q.commonError: Uses the net AD shift as if it were the gross multiplier effect.
q.feedback: The gross increase is 80/(1−0.75) = $320 billion. The total AD offset is 320−230 = $90 billion. It already incorporates induced spending effects and does not receive another multiplier.

q.q: Government purchases rise by $80 billion and MPC is 0.75. Crowding out reduces aggregate demand by a total of $100 billion after induced spending effects. Using the simple spending multiplier, what is the net increase in AD?
options: $220 billion
$300 billion
$320 billion
$420 billion
q.commonError: Ignoring crowding out after applying the multiplier.
q.feedback: The gross AD increase is 80/(1−0.75) = $320 billion. Subtract the already-total AD offset once: 320−100 = $220 billion. Multiplying the $100 billion again would apply induced effects twice.

q.q: If government spending rises by $80 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the simple multiplier and total AD increase before crowding out?
options: Multiplier = 4; AD increase = $320 billion
Multiplier = 3; AD increase = $240 billion
Multiplier = 0.75; AD increase = $60 billion
Multiplier = 1.33; AD increase = $106.4 billion
q.commonError: multiplying by MPC instead of the multiplier
q.feedback: Multiplier = 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4. Total AD increase = 4 x $80 billion = $320 billion.

q.q: If MPC = 0.9 and government spending increases by $25 billion, what is the simple multiplier effect on AD before crowding out?
options: $250 billion
$22.5 billion
$27.8 billion
$225 billion
q.commonError: using 0.9 as the multiplier instead of 10
q.feedback: With MPC = 0.9, the multiplier is 10. AD increases by 10 x $25 billion = $250 billion.

q.q: If MPC = 0.5, the government purchases multiplier is:
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so 1/(1-0.5)=2.

q.q: The multiplier effect means an initial spending increase can raise AD by:
options: More than the initial spending
Exactly zero
Only less than the initial spending
Only changing SRAS
q.feedback: The multiplier occurs when spending creates additional rounds of income and consumption.

q.q: The multiplier effect means an initial increase in government spending can:
options: Create a larger total increase in aggregate demand and output
Affect only the first recipient of spending
Reduce GDP by the same amount
Shift LRAS immediately
q.feedback: Initial spending becomes income for others, whose further spending magnifies the total effect.

q.commonError: Using MPC as the multiplier.
q.q: The simple spending multiplier equals:
options: MPC
1 - MPC
MPC / 100
q.feedback: The multiplier is 1 divided by 1 minus MPC.

q.commonError: Using MPC directly as the multiplier.
q.q: If MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is:
Government spending rises by $20 billion and the multiplier is 3. Before crowding out, AD rises by:
options: $60 billion
$20 billion
$23 billion
$6.7 billion
q.feedback: The multiplier effect is $20 billion x 3 = $60 billion.

q.commonError: Stops at the first-round fiscal impulse and treats it as the full aggregate-demand effect.
q.q: Government purchases rise $50 billion and MPC is 0.75. Which statement correctly connects the fiscal action to the multiplier concept?
options: The $50 billion first-round AD impulse is magnified to $200 billion before any crowding-out offset.
The $50 billion first-round impulse remains $50 billion because later spending rounds do not affect AD.
The multiplier reduces the initial AD impulse to $37.5 billion.
The fiscal action shifts LRAS rather than aggregate demand.
q.feedback: After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect.

q.q: A tax cut occurs while households expect future taxes to rise and save much of the extra income. What happens to the tax multiplier?
options: It is weaker than simple models predict
It becomes infinite automatically
It shifts SRAS instead of AD
It eliminates crowding out
q.commonError: Assuming every tax cut creates the same consumption response.
q.feedback: If households save much of the tax cut, the increase in consumption and AD is weaker.

q.q: A government increases purchases by $50 billion and raises taxes by $50 billion. MPC is 0.75. Before subsequent multiplier rounds, the net first-round AD change is:
options: No change.
A $12.5 billion increase.
A $37.5 billion decrease.
A $100 billion increase.
q.commonError: Assuming equal spending and tax changes have equal direct AD effects.
q.feedback: Purchases add $50 billion; the tax increase cuts consumption by $37.5 billion.

q.q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $160 billion. Households spend 60 percent of the increase initially. If later rounds follow a simple spending multiplier of 2.5, the total AD increase before other offsets is:
options: $400 billion.
$64 billion.
$240 billion.
$96 billion.
q.commonError: Applying the multiplier to the full tax cut instead of the first-round consumption change.
q.feedback: First-round consumption rises $96 billion; multiplying by 2.5 gives $240 billion.

q.q: Households have an MPC of 0.75. One policy cuts taxes by $60 billion; an alternative raises government purchases by $45 billion. With the same spending multiplier and no crowding out, how do the policies' effects on aggregate demand and their budget costs compare?
options: Both first-round impulses are $60 billion and total shifts $240 billion, because taxes and purchases are identical
The tax cut adds only $45 billion in total, while purchases receive induced spending
Both first-round impulses are $45 billion and total shifts $180 billion, although the budget costs differ
The tax cut first adds $60 billion and ultimately $240 billion, while purchases add only $180 billion
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both first-round impulses are $60 billion and total shifts $240 billion, because taxes and purchases are identical” in this fiscal policy and aggregate demand task.
q.feedback: The tax cut initially raises consumption by 0.75 × $60 billion = $45 billion. Purchases also add $45 billion directly. Multiplying each by 4 gives $180 billion in total, but the tax cut costs the budget $60 billion versus $45 billion for purchases.

q.q: A $40 billion tax cut raises disposable income and MPC is 0.75. Before later multiplier rounds, how much does consumption increase?
options: $30 billion.
$40 billion.
$10 billion.
$53.3 billion.
q.feedback: The first-round consumption effect equals the change in disposable income times MPC.
q.commonError: Treats the full tax cut as immediate consumption.

q.q: The government reduces purchases $20 during a recession. With spending multiplier 2 and no offsets, how does this affect the existing demand shortfall?
options: It widens the shortfall by $10
It has no effect because purchases are transfers
It widens the shortfall by $40
It narrows the shortfall by $40
q.feedback: The negative purchases impulse is multiplied:−20×2=−40. It reinforces a demand recession.
q.commonError: Treats a purchases cut as expansionary demand policy.

q.q: Money growth rises from 8 percent to 20 percent. Velocity growth is zero and output growth is 4 percent. If expected inflation adjusts fully, what happens to nominal rates when the real rate stays at 3 percent?
options: Nominal rates rise from about 7 percent to about 19 percent.
Nominal rates fall from 7 percent to 3 percent.
Nominal rates rise from 8 percent to 20 percent exactly.
Nominal rates stay at 3 percent.
q.commonError: not converting money growth into inflation before applying Fisher
q.feedback: Inflation rises from 8 - 4 = 4 percent to 20 - 4 = 16 percent. With real rate 3 percent, nominal rates rise from 7 to 19 percent.

q.q: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. Equilibrium dollar quantity falls, but the final exchange rate is unavailable. If both curves shifted left, what additional evidence determines whether the dollar appreciated?
options: At the original exchange rate, whether the fall in quantity supplied exceeds the fall in quantity demanded
Whether both original curves had the same slope sign
Whether dollar quantity fell, since that alone determines appreciation
Whether demand shifted before supply, regardless of final curves
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Whether both original curves had the same slope sign” in this foreign exchange market task.
q.feedback: At the old exchange rate, a larger supply contraction creates excess demand, requiring a higher foreign-currency-per-dollar rate. A larger demand contraction creates excess supply. Final quantity alone does not identify the rate.

q.q: A report claims that dollar demand did not change between A and B because the final exchange rate is unchanged. What does the diagram show, and does it reveal which market shift occurred first?
options: Quantity rises from 100 to 150 and D1 differs from D0; the final equilibrium does not identify the order of the shifts.
Quantity rises from 100 to 200 and D1 differs from D0; the unchanged final rate proves demand shifted first.
Quantity rises from 100 to 200, but an unchanged exchange rate means the demand curve remained fixed.
Quantity rises from 100 to 200 and D1 differs from D0; the final equilibrium does not identify the order of the shifts.
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “S1 differs from S0, proving demand did not change; the final rate identifies supply first” in this foreign exchange market task.
q.feedback: The figure shows both curves shifting right and quantity doubling from 100 to 200 at rate 1.0. Offsetting effects on the rate do not mean unchanged demand. The final curves reveal no chronology.
q.imageAlt: Dollar demand and upward-sloping supply both shift right, from D0 and S0 to D1 and S1.

q.q: Use the foreign-exchange model in which net capital outflow determines a vertical supply curve for domestic currency. The domestic real interest rate rises, while a separate increase in risk makes investors want to send more funds abroad at each interest rate. The final currency-supply curve lies to the right of its original position. With domestic and foreign price levels fixed and demand for domestic currency unchanged, what does this tell us about the two effects on net capital outflow and the exchange rate?
options: The interest-rate rise caused the supply increase, reversing the usual NCO slope
Risk outweighs higher interest rates; the currency depreciates, but neither effect's size can be determined separately
Vertical supply means NCO is fixed across both equilibria, so the stated curve change is impossible
The effects of risk and the higher interest rate cancel exactly because both supply curves are vertical
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The interest-rate rise caused the supply increase, reversing the usual NCO slope” in this foreign exchange market task.
q.feedback: A vertical currency-supply curve fixes the quantity supplied for a given level of net capital outflow, not when that level changes. The rightward shift means the increase caused by risk exceeds the decrease caused by the higher interest rate. With currency demand unchanged, the domestic currency depreciates. The final shift alone does not reveal the size of each separate effect.

q.q: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. At the original exchange rate, an export-demand shock increases dollars demanded by 70 units and an asset-purchase shock increases dollars supplied by 45 units. What happens to equilibrium e and quantity, and do those two shift amounts identify their exact changes?
options: Both rise; e rises exactly 25 percent
e falls and quantity rises; supply determines the rate independently
Both rise; curve slopes are needed for exact changes
e is unchanged and quantity rises exactly 115 units
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both rise; e rises exactly 25 percent” in this foreign exchange market task.
q.feedback: At the old rate, excess demand is 70 − 45 = 25 units, so e rises. Both rightward shifts increase equilibrium quantity. Horizontal shift amounts at a common rate sign the change but do not determine exact rate or quantity changes without slopes.

q.q: Compare demand-first and supply-first adjustment from the solid to the dashed curves. Each market clears before the second shift. Approximately how do the intermediate exchange rates differ, and does the order change the final equilibrium?
options: Demand first gives 1.4 and supply first 0.6; both paths end at B once both shifts occur.
Demand first gives 1.2 and supply first 0.8; both paths end at B once both shifts occur.
Demand first gives 1.2 and supply first 0.8; these different temporary rates imply different final equilibria.
Both intermediate rates are 1.0; an unchanged final rate rules out a temporary exchange-rate response.
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both paths temporarily raise the rate because final quantity is larger” in this foreign exchange market task.
q.feedback: D1 intersects S0 near 1.2, while D0 intersects S1 near 0.8. The two sequences therefore have different temporary rates but the same final D1-S1 intersection at B. Endpoint evidence cannot establish an unchanged path.

q.q: In the NCO-based FX model, NCO is fixed. A student says a higher exchange rate must increase the quantity supplied. Which correction distinguishes a movement along vertical supply from a shift?
options: Moving up the vertical supply curve raises both NCO and supplied quantity
A higher exchange rate shifts vertical supply right even with NCO fixed
Moving along vertical supply requires an increase in foreign demand at every rate
Moving up the vertical supply curve leaves quantity fixed; changing NCO shifts that curve
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Moving up the vertical supply curve raises both NCO and supplied quantity” in this foreign exchange market task.
q.feedback: A vertical supply curve contains multiple exchange rates at one quantity. Moving along it does not change NCO; a change in NCO moves the whole curve horizontally. A separate demand shift can produce a new equilibrium rate at the same supplied quantity.

q.q: A country raises money growth from 5 percent to 25 percent while real output growth stays at 3 percent and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 2 percent to about 22 percent.
It rises from about 5 percent to about 25 percent exactly.
It falls from 25 percent to 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth is unchanged.
q.commonError: forgetting to subtract real output growth
q.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth: initially 2 percent, then 22 percent.

q.q: A government prints money to finance deficits. Money growth rises from 6 percent to 26 percent, output growth remains 3 percent, and velocity is stable. What happens to predicted inflation?
options: It rises from about 3 percent to about 23 percent.
It rises from about 6 percent to about 26 percent exactly.
It falls from about 23 percent to about 3 percent.
It stays at 3 percent because output growth did not change.
q.commonError: forgetting to subtract output growth from money growth
q.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is roughly money growth minus output growth. It rises from 3 percent to 23 percent.

q.q: Government finances $160 of purchases by creating money. With stable velocity and fixed long-run real output, an official calls this costless finance because no statutory tax bill is issued. What would a comparison of households with different cash holdings reveal?
options: All households bear equal real losses because the government purchase amount is the same for everyone.
Existing money holders lose purchasing power as prices rise; larger unprotected money balances create greater exposure even without a tax bill.
No household loses purchasing power because money creation adds the same amount of real output as the purchases.
Only borrowers lose purchasing power, while holding currency fully protects households from inflation.
q.commonError: Incorrect inference: Government gains real resources directly; creating money leaves existing purchasing power intact.
q.feedback: Money financing gives government a claim on real goods under the stated output constraint. Inflation erodes M/P for existing money holders. The burden depends on balances and timing rather than equal statutory assessments, so absence of a tax bill does not establish costless finance.

q.q: A student says a tax cut always creates the full multiplier effect. Which correction is best?
options: The final AD shift depends on MPC, saving, expectations, and crowding out.
The final AD shift ignores MPC because taxes only affect SRAS.
The final AD shift must equal zero because fiscal policy cannot shift AD.
The final AD shift becomes infinite when interest rates rise.
q.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as the guaranteed final effect.
q.feedback: The simple multiplier can be weakened by saving behavior, expectations, and crowding out.

q.q: A country doubles money growth, but output growth also rises sharply and velocity falls. Which warning is strongest?
options: Do not infer inflation from money growth alone when V and Y change.
Inflation must double because money growth always maps one-for-one.
Inflation must be zero because output growth always dominates.
Inflation must equal velocity growth because money is neutral.
q.commonError: Using money growth alone without velocity and output.
q.feedback: The quantity equation requires considering money growth, velocity growth, and real output growth together.

q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Inflation is approximately 9% and the nominal rate 11%; velocity and real output are irrelevant” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
q.q: A government finances spending through money creation. In the subsequent long-run comparison, money grows 9%, velocity falls 2%, and real output grows 3%. Use the growth-rate approximation; expected inflation adjusts to that result while the expected real rate stays 2%. Which inflation/interest interpretation is supported?
options: Inflation is approximately 9% and the nominal rate 11%; velocity and real output are irrelevant
Inflation is approximately 10% and the nominal rate 8%; subtract the real rate from inflation
Inflation is approximately 4% and the nominal rate 2%; expected inflation never affects nominal rates
Inflation is approximately 4% and the nominal rate approximately 6%; neither follows from money growth alone
q.feedback: Approximate inflation is gM+gV−gY=9−2−3=4%. With expected inflation adapting and real rate fixed at 2%, Fisher gives nominal interest≈2+4=6%. Money financing can affect both real balances and nominal returns through these specified channels.

q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The reserve injection raises real productive capacity immediately by the textbook deposit maximum” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
q.q: A banking system receives $110 of reserves. With a required reserve ratio of 10%, the simple model predicts a maximum deposit increase of $1100; actual deposits increase by $440. Interest rates fall, but firms also expect lower returns on their projects. Why might both deposit growth and investment spending be smaller than the simple model predicts?
options: The reserve injection raises real productive capacity immediately by the textbook deposit maximum
Leakages can explain a multiplier below ten, and weaker expected returns can further limit investment despite lower rates
The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible
Lower rates guarantee the full predicted investment expansion even when expected returns deteriorate
q.feedback: Observed multiplier=440/110=4, below the restrictive simple maximum 10. Even if rates fall, the rate-to-investment link can weaken when expected profitability falls. These are distinct constraints at successive stages.

q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Velocity growth is+3%; the nominal rate is 9%” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
q.q: Use the growth-rate approximation to the quantity equation, MV = PY. Money growth is 10%, output growth 3%, and inflation 4%. A report assumes stable velocity and predicts a nominal interest rate of 9% with a 2% real rate. What are velocity growth and the nominal interest rate when expected inflation equals actual inflation?
options: Velocity growth is +3%; the nominal rate is 9%
Velocity growth is 0%; the nominal rate is 12%
Velocity growth is −9%; the nominal rate is 2%
Velocity growth is −3%; the nominal rate is 6%
q.feedback: From π=gM+gV−gY, 4=10+gV−3 gives gV=−3. With expected inflation 4 and real interest 2, Fisher gives nominal 6.

q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
q.q: A banking system receives $350 of reserves. With a required reserve ratio of 10%, the simple model predicts a maximum deposit increase of $3500; actual deposits increase by $1400. Interest rates fall, but firms also expect lower returns on their projects. Why might both deposit growth and investment spending be smaller than the simple model predicts?
options: Leakages can explain a multiplier below ten, and weaker expected returns can further limit investment despite lower rates
The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible
Lower rates guarantee the full predicted investment expansion even when expected returns deteriorate
The reserve injection raises real productive capacity immediately by the textbook deposit maximum
q.feedback: Observed multiplier=1400/350=4, below the restrictive simple maximum 10. Even if rates fall, the rate-to-investment link can weaken when expected profitability falls. These are distinct constraints at successive stages.

q.q: The economy is below potential. Congress increases purchases, but the resulting rise in interest rates reduces private investment. Which conclusion best combines the multiplier, crowding out, and AD-AS effects?
options: Aggregate demand can still rise, but crowding out makes the increase smaller than the simple multiplier predicts.
Crowding out guarantees aggregate demand falls below its starting position after every increase in government purchases.
The fiscal multiplier becomes exactly zero whenever market interest rates rise after expansionary policy.
Higher government purchases shift long-run aggregate supply right by the full amount of the simple multiplier.
q.commonError: Applying the simple fiscal multiplier without allowing for an interest-rate offset.
q.feedback: Fiscal expansion pushes AD right, but higher interest rates can crowd out some private investment, making the realized AD increase smaller than the simple multiplier predicts.

q.q: A banking system receives $230 of reserves. With a required reserve ratio of 10%, the simple model predicts a maximum deposit increase of $2300; actual deposits increase by $920. Interest rates fall, but firms also expect lower returns on their projects. Why might both deposit growth and investment spending be smaller than the simple model predicts?
options: Leakages can explain a multiplier below ten, and weaker expected returns can further limit investment despite lower rates
The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible
Lower rates guarantee the full predicted investment expansion even when expected returns deteriorate
The reserve injection raises real productive capacity immediately by the textbook deposit maximum
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
q.feedback: Observed multiplier=920/230=4, below the restrictive simple maximum 10. Even if rates fall, the rate-to-investment link can weaken when expected profitability falls. These are distinct constraints at successive stages.

q.q: Compare two long-run money-growth cuts of 4 points. In A, output and velocity growth stay fixed and expectations fully adjust. In B, velocity growth rises 4 points while output growth stays fixed. Real interest rates are unchanged. Which comparison follows under the growth and Fisher approximations?
options: Both inflation and nominal interest fall 4 points in both economies because money growth alone determines them
A’s real interest falls 4 points; B’s nominal interest falls 8 points
Both economies’ real output growth must fall 4 points to absorb the policy
A’s inflation and nominal interest fall 4 points; B’s velocity offset leaves both unchanged
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both inflation and nominal interest fall 4 points in both economies because money growth alone determines them” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
q.feedback: In A, Δπ=−4, so the expected-inflation component of nominal interest falls 4. In B, ΔgM+ΔgV=−4+4=0; unchanged inflation expectations imply unchanged nominal rates at the fixed real rate.

q.q: Private saving is $420 billion, public saving is −$80 billion, and domestic investment is $390 billion. What follows?
options: National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are $50 billion
National saving is −$50 billion, so NCO and NX are −$390 billion
National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are −$50 billion
National saving is $500 billion, so NCO and NX are $110 billion
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are $50 billion” in this international transactions and identities task.
q.feedback: National saving is $420 billion − $80 billion = $340 billion. Subtracting $390 billion of investment gives NCO = NX = −$50 billion.

q.q: A deficit lowers public saving $74 billion. Private saving rises by an unknown amount, domestic investment falls $22 billion, and NX falls $31 billion. Which private-saving response and interpretation reconcile the accounts?
options: Private saving rises $43 billion; NX must fall by the full deficit increase
Private saving falls $21 billion; investment crowding out enlarges the NX decline
Private saving rises $105 billion; the deficit necessarily produces a trade surplus
Private saving rises $21 billion; the NX decline is smaller than the deficit increase
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Private saving rises $43 billion; NX must fall by the full deficit increase” in this international transactions and identities task.
q.feedback: Let p be the private-saving rise. ΔNX = (p − 74) − (−22) = p − 52 = −31, so p = 21. Offsetting private saving and lower investment both cushion the external-balance effect.

q.q: Private saving rises $40 billion, public saving falls $15 billion, and domestic investment rises $10 billion. The trade accounts report exports up $20 billion and imports up $10 billion. Under S−I=NX, with no statistical discrepancy and all saving/investment figures held fixed, which correction makes the trade figures consistent with saving and investment?
options: NX must rise $35 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must fall $15 billion
NX must fall $15 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must rise $35 billion
NX must rise $15 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must rise $5 billion
NX must rise $10 billion; revise saving down $5 billion despite the instruction to hold it fixed
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “NX must rise $35 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must fall $15 billion” in this international transactions and identities task.
q.feedback: National saving rises 40−15=25; subtract investment growth 10 to obtain NX growth 15. Since ΔNX=ΔX−ΔM, 15=20−ΔM implies imports rise 5. The original trade report's $10 billion NX increase fails the identity under the stated constraints.

q.q: A larger budget deficit lowers public saving while private-saving behavior and investment determinants remain unchanged. Which complete loanable-funds sequence follows?
options: National saving falls, investment demand shifts left, and both the rate and quantity fall
National saving rises, supply shifts right, and investment falls along demand
National saving is unchanged because public saving is not part of loanable-funds supply
Supply shifts left, raising the rate and reducing investment
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving falls, investment demand shifts left, and both the rate and quantity fall” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
q.feedback: Public saving is part of national saving, which supplies loanable funds. A deficit lowers that supply, raises the equilibrium real interest rate, and crowds out investment along unchanged demand.

q.q: At every given real interest rate, public saving falls by $30 billion while planned private saving rises by $10 billion. With investment demand unchanged, what follows?
options: Supply shifts left, raising the rate and reducing investment
National saving rises $40 billion, shifting supply right and increasing investment
National saving falls $20 billion, shifting investment demand left and lowering the rate
National saving remains unchanged because private saving always offsets a deficit
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving rises $40 billion, shifting supply right and increasing investment” in this loanable funds shifts task.
q.feedback: The component changes sum to −$20 billion. Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left, which raises the equilibrium real rate and reduces investment along demand.

q.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the lines are straight. A fiscal change lowers public saving by $55 billion at every real rate, while a separate incentive raises planned private saving by $15 billion at every rate. Investment demand does not shift. Which comparison correctly connects the policy shifts with A and B?
options: Saving supply shifts left $40 billion, while investment falls $30 billion; the higher rate induces some additional saving.
Saving supply shifts left $40 billion, while investment falls $20 billion; the higher rate induces some additional saving.
Saving supply shifts left $40 billion and investment falls $20 billion; the remaining $20 billion is a rightward shift of investment demand.
Saving supply shifts left $20 billion and investment falls $40 billion; the equilibrium change measures the fixed-rate supply shift.
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Saving supply shifts left by $20 billion, and equilibrium investment falls by $40 billion” in this loanable funds shifts task.
q.feedback: At any given rate, the saving-supply change is −55 + 15 = −$40 billion, matching the horizontal distance between S0 and S1. The marked equilibria move from 100 to 80, so investment falls by $20 billion. The higher rate partly offsets the supply reduction by inducing additional saving along the shifted schedule.

q.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion. The straight S0 and S1 curves capture a fiscal change, with the private-saving schedule unchanged and D0 fixed. Starting from B, a second policy raises planned private saving by $15 billion at every real rate. How much must public saving rise from its level at B to restore A?
options: $45 billion; together with the $15 billion private-saving increase, this restores a 60-unit supply shortfall.
$5 billion; adding the $15 billion private increase to the 20-unit equilibrium gap restores the original supply schedule.
$55 billion; the private-saving increase must be added to, rather than deducted from, the 40-unit shortfall.

Private saving supplies $15 billion of that shift, leaving $25 billion of public saving. With D0 fixed, restoring S0 restores A.

q.q: Expected investment profitability falls while a budget deficit also reduces national saving. What must happen, and what remains uncertain?
options: The real rate falls, while equilibrium quantity is ambiguous
Quantity falls; the real-rate direction is ambiguous
Both the real rate and quantity must rise
The real rate must remain unchanged, while quantity falls
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real rate falls, while equilibrium quantity is ambiguous” in this loanable funds shifts task.
q.feedback: Investment demand shifts left and loanable-funds supply shifts left. Both changes reduce equilibrium quantity, but demand puts downward pressure on the rate while supply puts upward pressure on it.

q.q: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the straight-line shifts summarize all changes in saving and investment behavior. Public saving falls by $10 billion at every real rate, while technology raises investment demand. What private-saving shift is required to reconcile the graph with that fiscal change?
options: Private saving must rise $70 billion: together with public saving falling $10 billion, this gives a $60 billion supply increase.
Private saving must rise $50 billion: together with public saving falling $10 billion, this gives the plotted $40 billion supply increase.
Private saving must rise $30 billion: subtract the $10 billion public-saving loss from the plotted $40 billion increase.
Private saving must rise $10 billion: an unchanged equilibrium rate implies no national-saving change.
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A $30 billion increase at every rate; subtracting the public-saving decline gives the $40 billion supply increase” in this loanable funds shifts task.
q.feedback: At 6 percent, S0 and D0 each have quantity 40, while S1 and D1 each have quantity 80. Each schedule shifts right by $40 billion. Since national saving combines private and public saving, the private shift must satisfy private change − 10 = 40, giving +$50 billion. The two shifts leave the depicted equilibrium rate at 6 percent.
